## If slow isn’t realistic for you

“Slow down” is good advice if you can actually do it. This whole article is mostly about me, but I don’t think this part is unusual.

How fast? It depends a lot on her, I guess. I went years without sex with one girl because she was a virgin. That’s one reason I like virgins: sex is really hard to have unplanned.

If she’s already really into sex, it can be quick. Men naturally love to please women, and it’s hard to break the mood and say, “Hey, sorry, I’m not so keen on sex yet,” when you’re highly turned on yourself. Heat of the moment, etc. Common problem.

So have the deeper conversations by phone or video first, or meet in person around other people. A meetup group, a friend’s event, whatever. Plan not to go home together, and tell her beforehand that you want to keep things less private at first. If you only say it when she asks you to come home, it sounds like rejection.

Islamic culture says a man and woman shouldn’t be alone together before marriage. Conservative Christians say similar things. I don’t accept their solution, but they noticed something real.

Still, if two people are alone, attracted, and turned on, obviously things may happen. And we don’t live in tribes anymore. The people around us usually don’t know both of us, and nobody is there slowing things down while we figure out what this actually is.

Plan for the horny, impulsive person you really are. Before meeting somebody you’re extremely attracted to, masturbate a lot. Then imagine you already had sex with her. How do you feel now? Keep that feeling in mind, especially when you get horny again.

Men should understand they actually do have safe birth-control options that work better than condoms, including Gandarussa herb, and it makes sense to use that. It doesn’t make impulsiveness okay. It just makes pregnancy a bit less likely. Emotional attachment is still just as likely.

If you do have sex quickly, at least don’t let everything else speed up at the same time. Keep socializing with other people together. Try to have some kind of community even if you aren’t in a real one.

Moving in together right away is generally a bad idea. You’re basically getting into common-law marriage without even asking for it. The Bible also says something, I think, about marriage beginning when you sleep in the same tent together.

This is one step that’s easier not to jump into unless you literally can’t pay the rent, because moving isn’t easy. Once you live together, momentum starts making decisions for you.

Formal check-ins help too. Otherwise it’s very easy to assume mind reading, fawn, or idealize how things are. Pick actual dates and ask how the relationship is going before there’s a crisis. Otherwise we’re just riding blind.

Wanting somebody doesn't tell me whether I should have children with her or build a life with her, and I can know the first part much faster than the second. A wonderful lover can still be a terrible co-parent, community member, or life partner. One of the stupid things my brain can do is turn “I'm taking a chance on her” into “she's the right person” after we've been together for a while. Based on what? Sometimes I actually learned something. Sometimes nothing changed except that now I'm attached, and the new certainty is just harder for me to question.

At some point one of you will ask, “Why am I special to you? Why are you with me and not somebody else?” If the answer is basically, “We had sex and got hitched?” I don’t know, that’s a damn shame.

### Slow steady may win the race, but turtles have problems too!

Going slowly can show you how somebody’s moods move over time, how they treat you, and how they treat other people. It still can’t tell you how good the sex will be or how either of you will act afterward.

You can know somebody for twenty years and then discover on the first night that the polarity isn’t there, touch feels wrong, smell feels wrong, your desire levels or kinks don’t fit, one person is sexually shut down, or the bodies just don’t connect.

Some of those things might get better if both partners are committed to helping each other through it, but tomorrow’s not a given and every situation is unique.

Bad sexual fit basically feels like, “Let’s just be friends!”

That conversation is hard because saying, “The sex isn’t working for me,” may sound like, “I only love you if the sex is good.” But universal love doesn’t make someone special. It isn’t romance. It’s the basis of any good relationship of any kind.

I can still love you and not want to be in a romantic relationship with you. Romantic love generally needs good sex too, or we’re friends who care deeply about each other.

So go slowly if you can. Just don’t imagine that means you know everything. You learn what you can before sex. Sex itself tells you other things.

## The conversation about flaws

I wouldn’t ask someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” That would be a pretty weird date.

But I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones. If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”

“I have baggage” tells me almost nothing. What are you having trouble with now? What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?

I’d want both of us to be honest about how effective we actually are at handling our own issues. What addictions or impulsive behaviors can’t we reliably control? How dependable are we? What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once? That tells me more than either of us announcing that we’re healed.

The most recent conflicts are the best place to look. Were you able to regulate at all during the conflict? What did you do to the other person? How did you repair afterward? What did you learn? Has your judgment gotten better, or do you keep falling for the same stuff?

And would your friends or exes recognize this improvement, or is it only true in your own autobiography? The people who actually went through the pattern with you might have a different review.

Name the effect on the other person too. “I shut down” is useful. “I shut down for days and made my partner feel abandoned” tells me much more.

My own list isn’t especially flattering. I’m impulsive. I idealize too much, although I don’t demonize. I’m very open and not very private. I care more about honesty than the standard romantic ideal. I still love my exes. After being deeply in love, I have overly high expectations, so I’m hard to please with a basic relationship.

I’m also extremely unique and have deeply held convictions many people won’t agree with. I’m anti-vax, anti-money, anti-civilization, etc. And I’m not yet living the way I want to live.

A woman should know that before she starts fitting me into the life or fantasy she already planned.

Key was an inner-child therapist and Reiki healer. Both Key and Bee were extremely curious and open-minded, which I loved about them. They were open to spiritual experiences, very connected to childlike wonder, meditated a lot, and were always seeing what they needed to work on. They both said those meditations helped them a lot.

I saw all that and thought anyone with that much spiritual depth and curiosity must already be far along on the path.

That was my mistake. The meditations may have helped them a lot. I still had no idea how either woman would act when a relationship got ugly. If somebody starts with enough trauma, huge progress can still leave a lot unresolved.

My own blind spot is that I have trouble understanding where people are at mentally and emotionally. A partner may agree with everything I say and then tell me later, “Didn’t you understand I was FAWNING?”

No. I didn’t understand. Don’t expect me to.

If you are fawning, tell me when you can. I may notice things other people miss and completely miss something that feels obvious inside you.

A formal exchange probably isn’t going to happen. This stuff is more likely to come up naturally while talking about an ex, a recent fight, childhood, jealousy, or some other relevant topic. Conversation-card games can help too.

You have to actually want to know this stuff while you’re getting to know somebody. Then when the opening comes up, go there instead of both trying to look good.

# Are you ready for the crucible?

I call relationship a crucible because I was thinking of Dr. David Schnarch’s Crucible Approach in [*Passionate Marriage*](https://www.crucible4points.com/books/passionate-marriage/). It flips standard couples therapy on its head. Where traditional therapy focuses on compromise, active listening, and making each other feel safe, Schnarch argued that long-term relationships are inherently high-heat pressure cookers designed to force individual psychological growth.

I didn’t know what a crucible was either. It’s basically a container where things get heated until they change.

That’s definitely what relationship does.

It showed me how vulnerable I actually am when I open my heart. It’s really easy to feel invulnerable and strong when you’re alone, or even just with friends. Taking off the masks and showing your inner child is a gamble, but it’s required if you want to go deeper in yourself and deeper with another person.

Living alone is easy in so many ways. I can make my bed whenever I want. When I have a girlfriend, making the bed in the morning can become one of the ways I show her I love her. If I don’t do it well, somehow it may become a bad omen that I don’t care about her.

It shouldn’t be that serious. It really can be.

Dealing with somebody else’s emotional insecurities can also be exhausting. It’s easy to feel free when I don’t have to do that. I actually don’t have that much skill with people, and this works fine until I’m in a romantic relationship and suddenly I’m expected to mind-read, notice every emotional shift, check in constantly, and understand what a silence means.

Relationship may activate wounds that were already there. Sometimes it may open a level of the heart that is simply very young and vulnerable, whether you knew there was a wound there or not. You become like a baby again. There’s a reason lovers call each other “baby” and “my baby.”

That can be an incredible therapy opportunity. Every such opportunity also carries a risk of failure and more trauma.

With Bee, Key, and H.D., there was always some sense that they were remembering how their dad treated them and judging me according to how close to him—or different from him—I was. That puts me in a tough position. I want to play the role they need in some way, but I don’t want to leave the reality of me being me.

A smaller example happened with all of them. They could message me whenever they wanted, even a day later. If I took a day to respond, suddenly it was weird. What was I doing? What did it mean?

The present issue may be tiny. The part reacting to it may be five years old.

Nobody has to be completely healed before entering a relationship. My standards used to be very low and now they are much higher because I’m exhausted by drama. Other people will have different standards.

At the very least, there needs to be honesty, real effort at improving, and some ability to stop blaming everybody else for your own problems.

[Inner-child reparenting](https://innerchild.u-dont-exist.com) is a big part of this. The present-day adult has to learn how to parent the child part instead of quietly hiring the partner for the job.

When that doesn’t happen, I see entitlement, lack of responsibility, assumptions that the partner should mind-read, little awareness of your own behavior patterns, and then denial when somebody calls the pattern out.

Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see.

A peer can give another angle. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive that a peer counselor hopefully does not.

That’s why I recommend [peer counseling](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/hearthwork-an-integrated-peer-counseling) outside the couple. Your partner should not have to be the only person who listens to your pain, helps you understand it, and absorbs the consequences when you don’t.

The body has to be included too. My mind may understand that my partner is going through something difficult and that I don’t have to be dragged down with her. Meanwhile my body feels dragged down, fragile, and sensitive. My breathing gets shallow. It becomes extremely hard to feel okay while she is in pain.

Crying helps a lot, but it may actually be harder for men once they are in a relationship because they are expected to be the shoulder everybody else cries on. That is another reason to have a peer counselor.

Breathwork is one of the easiest ways I know to calm down. Reduced breathing or the Buteyko method is especially useful to me when my partner is getting me upset and flustered with drama. Sometimes she’s deliberately trying to do that. Other times it’s hard to tell. I explain more of the body-based options in my [Somatic Modalities guide](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/somatic-modalities-strategic-sequencing).

[NATIVE SUBSTACK PREVIEW — Somatic Modalities Strategic Sequencing Roadmap — https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/somatic-modalities-strategic-sequencing]

Meditation matters a lot to me too. For most people I would still put inner-child reparenting, peer counseling, and body-based work first. Many people say they cannot meditate or have not gotten to that stage yet. Meditation is also an easy road into spiritual bypassing, so it is a double-edged sword.

Relationship itself can grow somebody who is not fully ready. Some wounds may not even appear until there is a person important enough to activate them. But “not fully ready” should still mean fairly ready, and there should be support outside the couple.

Before entering something serious, have the conversation about flaws. You don’t need to announce that you are healed. The crucible will find out anyway.

## Don’t make your partner your whole world

When I’m in love, my partner is my everything. Everything else drops away. I still try to make some time for friends, but really all I want to do is be with her.

That little paradise is wonderful, but it contains the seed of its own destruction. Part of why it feels like a magical wonderland is that you can suddenly stop parenting yourself now that you have someone who's fully got your back. This makes you soft and weak, kinda like a sweet treat or heroin. It is wonderful to have their love and support, but don't let that bring you away from your own self-love, reparenting, meditation, yoga, and other healing practices that keep you independently healthy. Otherwise, you'll end up blaming them when you feel bad.

So don't let your world get so small. Don’t abandon your friends unless they really aren’t good for the relationship. And if they aren’t, ask why. Are they bad friends? Are they slyly interested in one of you romantically? Or is the relationship so weak that it can’t handle anybody with an outside view?

You don’t need to spend as much time with friends as you did before the romance. But keep some room to explore life on your own.

For me, that also means keeping close friends, outside therapy when I need it, a mission of my own, separate interests, some connection to community, and the ability to be alone.

It’s better to schedule some alone time than to suddenly announce, “I need time for myself!” when you’re already overwhelmed and make it sound like the relationship is the problem.

And proactively bring each other out into the world. Don’t sequester each other like a hidden treasure.

## When you and your partner are at different levels of maturity

While different maturity levels are to be expected to some degree, it can get out of hand at the extremes. What I noticed in all three of my reference relationships, is when one person is always the child and the other is always the therapist, guru, doctor, or dad, then it’s too unequal, and eventually there will be some kind of pendulum swing or backlash. When I became consistently the responsible one, that also made me responsible for everything that went wrong, not to mention the unhealthy clinginess, jealousy, and all the rest which went along with that dynamic.

All three women told me at some point that they felt like my patient. Which is true, I really was the one they asked about almost every medical, mental-health, and practical problem:

“I’m sick. What should I take?”

“I’m sad. What should I do?”

Of course I helped. Saying, “I’m not your doctor or therapist,” every time would have been cold. But enough moments become a pattern.

Key at first asked me innocently, "Can you be my guru?" I told her, “I’m not anyone's guru, but we can learn from each other.” A few months later, she was telling me she was much more spiritually advanced than me. I asked, “Do you recall asking me to be your guru?” She said, "Wow, I must have been really confused back then!"

I also have to admit, I can become condescending when somebody stops taking responsibility for their behavior. I find that intolerable. If someone says, “I feel like your patient,” both people need to look at their roles.

I know what can happen on my side. Helping feels good. Being needed can feel good too. A lot of the time I really did have the information or perspective they needed, so of course they kept asking me. I also had to look at whether they were trying to take care of themselves without me.

### Different levels in different domains can be complementary

According to me, myself, and Irene, I was ahead of Bee, Key, and H. in maturity, emotional stability, self-love, and self-awareness. I also had advantages they didn’t, including a happier childhood and more moolah. As you might imagine, all of that affected the balance between us.

They were all ahead of me in childlike wonder and fascinating creative intuition, which is what attracted me. Sometimes their intuition was wrong and they trusted it too much, but I still loved that quality in them, since I tend to be more analytical.

They were also all more social than me. They could organize people for a ceremony or group gathering very easily. I felt like I needed that if I ever wanted to start a commune, because I’m more introverted.

I’m good at talking to people when there’s a purpose. I’m not as good at rousing everybody up and encouraging them to do things or go places with me. I’m more like, “Everyone can do whatever they want.”

So I do believe in mutual coaching and complementarity.

I could teach these women about loving and reparenting their inner child, Buddhism, meditation, and other things I understood better. They could pull me into life more, show me where I was missing people, and sometimes be the skeptic when I was seeing the best in someone and missing their hidden motives.

The roles can flip, teacher one day, student the next. That’s healthy. A partner can comfort you, teach you, protect you, or carry more for a while, but they can’t permanently take over the job of reparenting your inner child. Each person still has to do that for themself, but that's easier said than done.

Once one person has become the default caregiver and that's taken for granted, it's time to bring in other support, lest the romance collapse under the burden. Maybe the romance actually does need less intensity, maybe it becomes friendship, or maybe it ends. I can't answer that for others, and I couldn't always answer it for myself, but asking the question out loud is usually where it starts.
